Trouble
TRUB-'l
n. and v. (rendering Hebrew tsārâh and 'ākar, and Greek thlipsis, tarassō)
From Old French trubler, ultimately from Latin turbidus, disturbed, muddied — the image is of clear water stirred up and made turbid. The Hebrew tsārâh comes from a root meaning narrow or straitened, so that trouble is pictured as a tight place, a constriction; and the Greek thlipsis is literally pressure, a pressing or squeezing. Between them the two languages give trouble two faces: it muddies, and it presses.

Biblical Definition

Scripture treats trouble as the settled condition of life under the curse rather than as an interruption of a normal calm. Job states it flatly: “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1). The Lord Jesus is equally plain and adds the remedy in the same breath: “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Joh 16:33) — the promise is not exemption but a conquered world and a cheerful heart within it. Because trouble is expected, the psalms do not treat it as evidence against God's care; they make it the occasion of His nearness: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1) — and the adjective matters, since the help is present rather than eventual. The same psalm draws the conclusion Scripture always draws from it: therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed. The Lord's own word to troubled disciples is a command about the heart with a prescribed cure: “Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me” (Joh 14:1) — the disturbance is to be answered by an act of faith in a Person, not by a change of circumstances, and He goes on to speak of the Father's house and of His coming again. Scripture also knows a trouble that men bring on themselves and others: Achan troubled Israel, and the valley of Achor is named for it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Distress, affliction, and pressure; in Scripture the ordinary condition of man under the curse and of the believer in the world, met not by exemption but by a very present help, an overcoming Lord, and a heart commanded to rest in Him.

TROUBLE, v.t. 1. To agitate; to disturb; to put into confused motion, as water. An angel went down and troubled the water. John 5.

2. To disturb; to perplex; to afflict; to grieve; to vex. Let not your heart be troubled. John 14.

3. To busy; to give occasion for labor; as, I will not trouble you further.

4. TROUBLE, n. Disturbance of mind; agitation; affliction; distress. Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward. Job 5.

5. In Scripture, the word answers to a Hebrew term signifying a strait or narrow place, and to a Greek term signifying pressure; whence God is said to set our feet in a large room, and to deliver out of straits.

Key Scripture

Job 14:1 — "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble."

Psalm 46:1 — "To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."

John 14:1 — "Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me."

John 16:33 — "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."

Modern Corruption

Two teachings share one error about trouble: the prosperity gospel says the believer should not have it, and a therapeutic Christianity says its only meaning is what it does for personal growth — both losing the biblical account of affliction as appointed, purposeful, and accompanied.

expand to see more

The prosperity teaching treats trouble as evidence of insufficient faith, so that the afflicted Christian is doubly burdened — by the affliction and by the verdict that he brought it on himself. Scripture forecloses this. The Lord promised tribulation in the world as a matter of course; Paul's résumé is stripes, prisons, shipwrecks, and a thorn in the flesh that was not removed after three requests; and Peter tells his readers not to think it strange concerning the fiery trial, as though some strange thing happened unto them. The doctrine of providence is the honest alternative: all things work together for good to them that love God, which is a promise about outcome under God's hand, not a promise of an untroubled passage.

The therapeutic misreading is gentler and now more common. It keeps trouble but reduces its meaning to personal growth, so that affliction is valuable insofar as it makes one stronger or more self-aware, and God is the facilitator of that development. Scripture's account is larger and less flattering. Affliction is chastening from a Father to sons, working the peaceable fruit of righteousness; it is fellowship with Christ's sufferings; it equips us to comfort others with the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted; and it is producing a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. Above all it is accompanied — when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee — and the presence, not the lesson, is the promise the psalms rest on.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsārâh pictures trouble as a narrow, straitened place, from tsārar, to bind or cramp; 'ākar is to trouble in the sense of stirring up and bringing disaster, as Achan did. Greek thlipsis is pressure, and tarassō is to agitate as water is stirred.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsārâh (H6869) — distress, straits, trouble; from tsārar, to be narrow. The word in Psa 46:1 and in Jacob's trouble (Jer 30:7).

Hebrew 'ākar (H5916) — to trouble, to stir up, to bring disaster; used of Achan, and giving the name of the valley of Achor (Jos 7:25-26).

Hebrew 'āmāl (H5999) — toil, mischief, sorrow; often rendered trouble, as in Psa 73:5, they are not in trouble as other men.

Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation; some 45 occurrences, from the tribulation of Joh 16:33 to the great tribulation of Rev 7:14.

Greek tarassō (G5015) — to agitate, stir, disturb; used of the troubled water at Bethesda, of Herod troubled at the wise men, and of the heart in Joh 14:1.

Usage

"Of the human condition: man that is born of a woman is full of trouble (Job 14:1); man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward (Job 5:7)."

"Of God's help within it: a very present help in trouble (Psa 46:1); call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee (Psa 50:15)."

"Of the commanded heart and the overcoming Lord: let not your heart be troubled (Joh 14:1); in the world ye shall have tribulation (Joh 16:33)."
